track: T1 — Silver-owned fixed capacities and an unbounded implementation design
summary:
I inventoried every fixed bound in the Silver-owned SPARK sources (recognizers, driver, report pipeline, Image adapter, platform, libraries, runtime library), the generated packages and the script mirrors. I measured the production `silver check` and scratch rebuilds of the recognizer at 4/16/64 KiB source limits, plus cheap GNAT -gnatc probes.

**4096 is four distinct domains, and the code conflates them.** Source length, String value length, argument length and length-literal value are all 4096. The String value domain is enforced through `Max_Source_Length` itself (`silver_output_profile.adb:593-594`, `Capacity_Value`, `Integer_Literals.Literal_Value`), and Lean's `maxSourceLength` serves both roles. Separating them is the first prerequisite.

**The recognizer has real superlinear behaviour today (observed):**
- **Nested-loop stack:** each nested loop copies two whole binding environments (29 KiB per level at 4096). In scratch builds this grows linearly with the source limit (113 KiB/level at 16 KiB, about 576 KiB/level at 64 KiB). Total stack is therefore O(S²): a 16 KiB nest needs about 64 MiB.
- **Condition parentheses take quadratic time:**
  - 1998 levels: 1.73–1.88 s at 4096 bytes.
  - 8142 levels: 32 s at 16 KiB, with 16.35 MiB of stack.
- **Base stack scales with the limit:** about 3.3 MiB at 64 KiB, before any nesting.
- **Declarations scale quadratically:** 4.9 s for 4000 declarations at 64 KiB. About two thirds of that is runtime checking of quantified preconditions under `-gnata`.
- **`compile` re-parses up to six times.**

All of this is fixable within SPARK. With run-time-sized environments, in-place loop-scope push/pop, procedure-based declarations, a bracket-matching table, name interning and a single scan, memory is O(S) and time O(S log S). Stack exhaustion then depends only on nesting depth (about 1–2 KiB per level). It can become memory exhaustion by raising RLIMIT_STACK to its hard limit (unlimited on this host) and re-executing, or by explicit heap work stacks.

**Report audit.** The 16 MiB retained buffer only covers sources up to 4502 bytes under the documented envelope. A growable heap buffer, with `Max_Report_Length` set to `Natural'Last - 1`, keeps the proved policy unchanged; only its constant changes, and there is no Lean impact. Beyond 2 GiB would need 64-bit-indexed byte arrays or streaming.

**Image adapter.** It has no Silver-chosen limit that grows with program size. Byte counts and depth are 63-bit. The only node-id cap is the producer's own 2^31−1 counter.

**Runtime value domain.** It can move to Ada's natural bound (V = Integer'Last, no argument cap) using 64-bit admission arithmetic and ghost sequences in `Silver_IO`. Membership becomes a strict superset of today's. Two risks remain: static data near 2 GiB in the native toolchain, and large dynamic Strings on the application stack.

**Resource failures are mis-reported today.** `Storage_Error` exits with status 1 in both `check` and `run`; in `run`, 1 is also the application's Reject status. I propose status 4 via a top-level SPARK `Storage_Error` handler, with an optional supervisor process.

**Tool-forced bounds:**
- **Exponent:** GNAT 16.1 rejects any exponent of 800,000 or more ("exponent too large"), in any base and with any mantissa. Silver's 4096 can rise to 799,999 but no further. Each literal at that limit costs 3.5–68 s of frontend CPU.
- **Line length:** the GNAT line limit becomes a required per-line rule once the total cap goes.

**Gate.** Whether the language may actually drop 4096, 64 and 63 is decided by T3/T4 evidence (frontend and solver completion), not by Silver code.
verdict:
Every Silver-owned fixed bound can be replaced so that the compiler fails only through resource exhaustion (heap, stack, time). This is tractable and provable in SPARK under the existing refinement pattern, at an XL cost dominated by redoing the Lean source certificates.

The only fixed bounds that must stay come from pinned tools or Ada itself:
- GNAT's maximum line length (per-line rule).
- GNAT's exponent limit: at most 799,999.
- The producer's 2^31−1 Image node counter.
- Ada's Natural/Positive String indexing, at about 2^31: retained reports up to `Natural'Last - 1`, values up to Integer'Last. Removing even this needs 64-bit byte arrays.

The 64-leaf and 63-operator budgets, and the 4096-byte source and value caps, are not needed by Silver's implementation. Whether membership may grow past them depends on external premises (T3 frontend capacity, T4 solver completion with no step or memory caps). Following the owner's rule, keep them until that research shows the larger language is tractable. Stages 0–2 below are safe now and change no membership.

items.name: Total source length 1..4096 bytes
items.role: Membership rule. It also implicitly bounds all recognizer storage, report size and VC size.
items.unbounded_replacement: No total cap; use Ada's natural bound Text'Length <= Positive'Last - 1 so the one-past cursor fits Natural. Read the source into a growable heap buffer; never reject on size. Replace with a per-line lexical bound forced by GNAT (separate item).
items.proof_impact: About 300 SPARK preconditions `Text'Length in 1 .. Max_Source_Length` change constant only. Cursor/Literal_Position become Natural-based. The Lean membership definitions (`decide (0 < length ∧ length ≤ maxSourceLength)` in about 10 admission modules) change, and 471 Lean uses must be split into source vs value roles.
items.risks: Unlocks the recognizer hot spots (stack O(S²), time O(S²)). The report envelope passes 16 MiB at S = 4503. VC size and solver completion grow with source (T4). GNAT frontend capacity premises for big sources (T3).
items.evidence: Lead facts. Stdout `Rejected` path at silver.adb:444-447. Scratch builds show base stack ∝ limit (L65536 about 3.3 MiB minimum).

items.name: Per-line length (new rule required if total cap is removed)
items.current_bound: Implicit; GNAT 16.1 rejects lines over its 32766-character limit
items.role: The pinned frontend must accept every admitted line. The Oracle forbids reformatting admitted source.
items.unbounded_replacement: None possible while GNAT 16.1 is pinned. Make it an explicit lexical rule: each line (bytes between LF/CR terminators) is at most GNAT's accepted maximum. Re-check on every toolchain change.
items.proof_impact: New decidable lexical predicate in the SPARK recognizer (linear scan) and in Lean membership. Replaces the total-length conjunct.
items.risks: Exact boundary and terminator semantics (CR, CRLF) must be pinned by T3 probes.
items.evidence: Lead: 'this line is longer than 32766 characters'; a 16,384-byte single line is accepted.

items.name: String value / intermediate length domain 4096
locations: Lean maxSourceLength used as value bound (StringLengths, PathBounds, ComposeSemantics, PredicateChecking ...)
items.role: Membership rule tying admitted values to Silver_IO's 4096 domain.
items.unbounded_replacement: V = Integer'Last, Ada's natural bound for one-based Strings; all admitted operands are one-based, so concatenation cannot raise Constraint_Error below V. Use Long_Long_Integer for Static + K*d: Static <= V (checked before each add), K <= S < 2^31 and d < 2^31, so K*d < 2^62.
items.proof_impact: Path_Facts/Length_Intervals subtypes become 64-bit. Recognizer value checks use a new Value_Limit constant, not Max_Source_Length. Lean needs a separate valueLimit, plus re-proof of every lemma that uses maxSourceLength as a value bound.
items.risks: Native static data near 2 GiB is unprobed: GNAT folds static Strings (2^27: 548 MB RSS) and emits about 2x value size in .o; small-code-model/relocation limits may make this a tool hard limit. Large dynamic Strings sit on the 8 MiB primary stack (environmental Storage_Error at application run time).

items.role: Runtime input domain and admission's input interval.

full_stops.issue: Admitting programs past 4096 bytes, 64 leaves or 63 operators makes the 'pinned solver completion' premise range over an infinite family of VC shapes. With a fixed --steps cap, a large enough admitted program would fail proof as a configured-cap defect, not through resource exhaustion.
full_stops.why: Solver completion cannot be proved in Lean or SPARK; it is a trusted premise (trusted-boundary.md first table). Silver-owned code can be made unbounded, but the language guarantee 'if it compiles, it proves' for unbounded programs rests on T4 evidence. Accepting that guarantee on an unverifiable premise over an infinite family is an assurance-policy choice.
full_stops.owner_action: No action needed under the stated rule (expand only as far as research shows is tractable). Default: keep the 4096-byte, 64-leaf and 63-operator membership limits until T3/T4 show frontend capacity and solver completion without step or memory caps. Act only if you want limits removed even where completion cannot be shown; that would be a deliberate widening of the documented premise.

premises: PREMISE (tool): pinned GNAT 16.1 accepts every admitted source line up to its maximum line length (rejects lines over 32766 characters, lead); a per-line rule is required once the total cap is removed.

PREMISE (tool, OBSERVED): pinned GNAT 16.1 rejects numeric exponents >= 800000 ('exponent too large') for bases 2, 10 and 16 and any mantissa, and accepts 799999 (0E799999 34 s, 16#0#E799999 68 s, 2#0#E799999 3.5 s of -gnatc CPU on this host).
PREMISE (tool): GNATprove/gnat2why/gnatwhy3 and the solvers complete for VCs of admitted programs of any size, without step or memory caps (T4). Not provable in Lean or SPARK.
PREMISE (tool): GNAT frontend tables, recursion and other internal limits do not reject large admitted sources (T3).
PREMISE (tool, unverified): the producer writes .spark through Natural-indexed strings, so raw reports stay below 2^31 bytes; then Natural'Last - 1 retained-report capacity never binds.
PREMISE (tool, documented): the Image producer's serialization counter is a Natural (<= 2^31-1); the adapter fails closed above it.
PREMISE (tool, unprobed): the native toolchain (GCC small code model, assembler, linker) accepts static String data up to the chosen value bound V; near 2 GiB this may be a hard limit.
PREMISE (environment): heap, stack (RLIMIT_STACK; hard limit unlimited here), time and disk suffice. Exhaustion is reported distinctly and never as nonmembership.

PREMISE (environment, OBSERVED): the GNAT runtime on Linux turns stack overflow into Storage_Error ('stack overflow or erroneous memory access'), which a handler can map to a resource-exhaustion status.
PREMISE (OS, OBSERVED): Linux per-argument limit 131071 bytes and ARG_MAX 2 MiB on this host. With no Silver argument cap these are environmental input bounds, not language rules.

PROVED (SPARK, current): executable recognizer functions equal their Static ghost models; the report policy over the projected buffer equals the unbounded raw-sequence policy (Application/Runtime_Projection_Correspondence) for any projected length up to the constant. The proposed changes keep these theorem shapes and change constants and representations.

LEGAL (SPARK RM 16.1 exceptions.rst:9-21): exception handlers without a choice parameter are permitted; GNATprove assumes language checks do not raise, so a Storage_Error handler is unverified-but-legal environmental handling.

track: T2 — Can the Lean assurance be generalized from the 4096-byte source/value bounds to unbounded or machine-bounded sources and values?
summary:
Yes, and the work is smaller than the 471 uses of `maxSourceLength` suggest. Almost no Lean proof uses the concrete value 4096. Only one group of theorems is actually true because of the bound: the conservative concatenation range schema checked against Ada's minimum Integer'Last of 32767.

I measured this directly. Each dependency cone was rebuilt in memory with the constant replaced by a free parameter, and every rebuilt declaration was kernel-checked against the frozen build. When a declaration failed, it was still added (unchecked) so that later declarations could be tested independently.
- **Run A** (`maxSourceLength := L`, `ScalarExpression.maxBindings := L/12`): 4,154 of 4,347 declaration groups check unchanged.
- **Run B** (the IO/argument `Max_Length` and 43 hard-coded 4096/4097 literals also set to L): 4,559 of 4,776 check.
- **Run C** (everything set to the concrete value 2,147,483,646, with Integer'Last := 2,147,483,647): 4,633 of 4,770 check. 67 of the 72 kernel-evaluated example theorems also pass at that size, so kernel computation does not grow with the bound.
- **Run D** (operand 64, operator 63 and exponent 4096 set to a parameter P): 2,524 of 2,627 check. The only extra requirement is P ≥ 1.

The remaining failures fall into these groups:
- **Compiler artifacts:** compiled `_unsafe_rec` copies and definitional `eq_1` lemmas.
- **Concrete examples:** true for any L at least as large as the example.
- **About 40 proofs that unfolded the constant:** they need only facts like 0 ≤ L, 16 ≤ L, 12 ≤ L, or a digit ≤ L.
- **Hard-coded literal copies:** 4096/4097 written directly into the OutputEquations/OutputExpressions structures and into `ScalarExpression.Native.ValidText/ResultType/LiteralType`.
- **Domain coupling:** `healthy_effect`, `selected_domain` and the `default_is_message` lemmas are true only because the source/value bound and the IO/argument `Max_Length` happen to both be 4096.
- **Truth-dependent arithmetic (5 declarations):** the range schema itself.

No decidability, uniqueness, termination, recognizer-fuel or Lean discharge-checker argument depends on the bound being finite.

`Current.ToolContract` contains no step, memory or time limit: `boundedProofCompletes` only asserts that some step count exists. The 100,000 steps and 1,000 MiB appear only in the driver (src/silver.adb:122) and the docs. So the Lean premise is already "the solvers complete given sufficient resources". The physical tool configuration is what narrows it.
verdict:
Generalizable without an Oracle amendment.
- **What can be proved:** with a symbolic bound, every top-level theorem (membership, decidability, unique meaning, safety and discharge, execution, pipeline, source correspondence) can be restated. The only side conditions are small lower bounds (L ≥ 16), the order between the separate bounds (argument ≤ value ≤ IO per call), and one arithmetic condition, V ≤ the target's Integer'Last. That last condition needs the exact range schema in place of today's uniform one; I proved the exact schema in a probe.
- **Truth-dependent today:** the uniform range schema `⟨L,L⟩` against Integer'Last 32767 holds only for L ≤ 16,383. The historical Guarded schema `⟨2L,L⟩` holds only for L ≤ 10,922. So even doubling the source bound to 16,384 makes `Current.uniform_discharge`, `automatic_discharge_complete` and `admitted_assurance` false unless the schema changes.
- **Value domain up to Integer'Last:** tractable once the String length arithmetic uses the pinned target's Integer'Last (2,147,483,647, which the scalar fragment already uses) and the exact `S + K*C ≤ V` schema.
- **Unbounded source text:** tractable for the language theorems. The tied correspondence to the native compiler stays machine-bounded: an Ada `String` index is at most Integer'Last, and GNAT has its 32,766-character line limit and 32-bit source positions. Those are inherited or hard tool limits, not arbitrary policy.
- **Solver resources:** removing or escalating the step and memory limits needs no Lean change.

track: T3 — Hard (non-resource) limits in the pinned toolchain (GNAT 16.1 frontend/backend, GNATprove 16.1/Why3/CVC5/Z3 4.15.4/Alt-Ergo 2.6.1) and Linux OS
summary:
I probed with gcc -gnatc and full -O0 compiles, gnatprove in check and flow mode, four tiny --mode=all runs to read the effective prover limits, kernel exec probes, and source reading of GCC 16.1 (gcc-mirror 6afcc4f6) and the spark2014/why3 producer (42554fc2). I found four limits that make an admitted program fail other than by resource exhaustion:
(1) GNAT physical line width. After expanding each tab to the next multiple of 8 columns, a line can be at most 32,765 columns. 32,765 bytes passes and 32,766 fails, with or without a terminator. With tabs, a 4,131-byte line already fails.
(2) Identifier length is at most 4,096 characters. 4,097 gives "GNAT BUG DETECTED Program_Error namet.adb:141 / Name buffer overflow; Max_Length = 4096" in every tested role and mode. This comes from namet.ads:144, where Bounded_String defaults to 2**12.
(3) Total source size near 2^31 bytes. 2^31-2^24 passes (10.5 s, 2.16 GB). 2^31-1 crashes with SIGSEGV and heap corruption. 2^31 makes gnat1 loop forever inside errout.
(4) In the proof configuration, --level=2 makes --memlimit=0 impossible: every prover process keeps a 1,000 MiB RLIMIT_AS (observed in why3session.xml). Dropping --level gives memlimit 0.
Also: Z3's rlimit wraps modulo 2^32, so any finite --steps above 5,368,146 silently gives Z3 a tiny limit. Prover crashes ('High failure'), including resource kills, are reported as 'gave_up', the same as a genuine 'unknown'.
Everything else I measured is resource-only: nesting depth, declaration and statement counts, total size up to 2 GB, backend size, and debug lines past 1.25M. The costs are stack, memory and time, mostly superlinear: gnatc time is quadratic in sequence length and nesting, and flow memory reaches 4.4 GB at 1 MB and 6.5 GB at 8,000 nested loops. Stack overflow appears as a GNAT bug box. gcc raises its own stack limit; gnat2why inherits 8 MiB and fails in flow mode between 1,000 and 2,000 nested loops (check mode between 2,000 and 8,000). All of these pass with an unlimited stack. OS limits are environmental: a single argument can be at most 131,071 bytes (one byte more gives E2BIG), and ARG_MAX is 2 MiB, set as stack/4.
verdict: Most of the expansive goal is reachable: everything I probed fails only through resources once the driver gives tools an unlimited stack and the proof command drops --level=2 (explicit provers, --memlimit=0, --timeout=0, --steps=0 or at most 5,368,146, -j at least 3). Three pinned-frontend limits are real hard tool limits and must become explicit, frontend-derived language rules once the 4096-byte source bound is lifted: (a) every physical line's tab-expanded width at most 32,765 columns; (b) identifier length at most 4,096 characters; (c) source length at most a derived bound below 2^31 (2,130,706,432 = 2^31-2^24 is the largest value tested). Ada String lengths at most Integer'Last are inherited semantics and must be a language bound as well. GNAT's fixed table capacities (Node_Id up to 2e9; List, Elist, Elmt, Name, String and Ureal ids 1e8 each) cannot be reached on this host before memory or time runs out. They should be stated as a tool premise; the only alternative is a much smaller source bound that I cannot derive rigorously. No Oracle-level full stop comes from T3 by itself, but the three frontend rules and the proof-limit change are language and assurance-text changes the lead must route through the normal amendment path.

items.name: GNAT physical line width (tab-expanded)
items.current_bound: Unreachable today: the 4096-byte source cannot contain a 4096-byte all-tab line plus program text. Frontend limit: tab-expanded width <= 32,765 columns; byte length <= 32,765.
locations: gnatsrc/scng.adb:129-190 (Check_End_Of_Line: Len > Max_Line_Length -> 'this line is too long'; if Len >= 4096, tab walk Col > 32766 -> 'this line is longer than 32766 characters' + Unrecoverable_Error)
items.role: The pinned frontend's representation of columns. It applies to gnat1 and to gnat2why, which uses the same scanner.
items.unbounded_replacement: None possible without patching GNAT or reflowing the source, which would break Sloc traceability. Minimal language rule: 'For every physical line (lines end at LF, CR or CRLF), the width after expanding each HT to the next column that is 1 more than a multiple of 8 is at most 32,765.' This implies at most 32,765 bytes per line. Literals and comments cannot span lines, so this rule also bounds them.
items.proof_impact: Needs a lexical predicate in Lean Admission and in the SPARK recognizer. It is a linear scan with a tab rule, so it is cheap to prove. It replaces the current frontend premise 'every line fitting 4096 bytes' with an exact derived bound. The bound is observed on the pinned binary and matches the source; it is a premise, not proved.
items.risks: The trigger is tab expansion, not byte count. A byte-only rule (<= 32,765) is wrong: a 4,131-byte line with tabs fails. The -gnatyM style switch would change the check; Silver passes no -gnaty. The source matches the fetched GCC tag, but binary identity is not attested.

track: T4 - Empirical proof scaling beyond 4096 bytes (production GNATprove via the Image adapter, -j8)
summary:
I ran 18 proof-mode GNATprove runs, one at a time, from 13:02 to 15:51. Each used the production Alire_Exec plus Image_Gnatprove command with -j8. Fifteen were scaling runs over three program families of 0.57 KB to 32.5 KB. F1 is mixed (loops, if/elsif, Image, concatenation). F2 is straight-line with context-dependent range and length checks. F3 is the known worst-case shape: dense String copies, one per line. Three more runs were small option smokes and an 8 KB dense memory probe. All 200 block instances, and every composite of 4096 bytes or less, printed "Accepted: silver." from silver check. Every completed run proved every check: exit 0, no unproved check, no crash, no hard tool error, and no check where every prover failed. The only flow messages were INEFFECTIVE warnings.

The largest completed results:
- f1-32k (32,461 bytes, 1,011 statements, 126 Main checks): 1,453 s, 5.15 GiB.
- f2-16k (16,279 bytes, 348 checks): 3,330 s, 4.86 GiB.
- f3-4k (4,096 bytes, 662 checks): 1,377 s, 5.86 GiB in gnatwhy3.

The 8 KB dense probe (f3-8k) was stopped by my own 14 GiB guard at 263 s while gnatwhy3 memory was still rising at about 50 MB/s. That is a resource stop, not a proof failure.

Growth exponents versus source size (log-log fit over runs of 1.5 KB or more):
- Wall time: 1.82 (F1), 1.99 (F2), 1.92 (F3), so roughly quadratic.
- gnatwhy3 peak memory: 1.00 (F1), 1.43 (F2), 1.98 (F3).
- Report bytes and check counts: about 1.0.

Per-check effort grows with program size because each check carries more context. Mean solver time per check rises steadily from the first to the last quartile of checks in every run. The worst single check took 0.06 s at 0.57 KB and 22.9 s at 32 KB. The largest step count from any prover rose from about 1.3k to 29k (F1, 4 KB to 32 KB) and to 54,409 (F2 16 KB). The winning prover (almost always Z3) used at most 1,021 steps (my runs) or 1,340 (earlier 4 KB reports). The 100,000-step budget therefore never bound.

The dominant cost is not solver search. It is the single-threaded vendor gnatwhy3 process, which processes every VC against the whole accumulated program context. CPU time roughly equals wall time, and solver time is small: 51 s of 1,377 s at f3-4k, 79 s of about 2,400 s in the earlier static800 report. Memory is allocated early and held. So -j has almost no effect, and the practical limit is time and RAM, which this profile accepts as resource exhaustion.

Two fixed caps showed up in the proof tool's own configuration:
1. Prover memory limit. With --level=2, --memlimit=0 is not unlimited: the vendor gnatwhy3 still receives "--memlimit 1000". An explicit --memlimit=16000 is passed through unchanged. At 32 KB, alt-ergo reached a sampled 0.905 GiB against that 1000 MB limit and failed 9 attempts ("High failure"). Z3 and CVC5 proved those checks, so nothing was left unproved. This is a fixed prover cap that larger programs will eventually hit. It is not exhaustion of the host.
2. Steps. --steps=0 is accepted and genuinely removes the step limit: provers run with no rlimit/steps-bound arguments.

Escalation to --steps=1000000 or 0 was never needed, because nothing was unproved.

All of this is host-specific observation under contention from the T2/T3 tracks. It is not proof and not a universal bound.
verdict:
Within the tested range nothing failed except by resource use. Every admitted-style program up to 32 KB (F1) and 16 KB (F2) proved fully under the unchanged production step budget. Cost is roughly quadratic in size and is dominated by single-threaded gnatwhy3 time and memory, not by the prover step budget. Dense straight-line code is the binding case: 4 KB takes about 23 min and 5.9 GiB; 8 KB passed 14 GiB within 4.4 minutes (projected about 23 GiB and about 85 min); 16 KB is projected near 90 GiB. Those limits are environmental resource exhaustion, which the profile accepts.

To make "fails only by resource exhaustion" true of the proof step itself, two configuration changes are needed. Both are cheap and need no Oracle amendment:
1. Replace the prover memory limit. --level=2 silently turns --memlimit=0 into 1000 MB. Pass an explicit large value, such as host physical memory, or an equivalent. The fixed 1000 MB is already making one of the three provers fail at 32 KB.
2. Handle the step budget. Either set --steps=0, which is confirmed unlimited, or retry any unproved check with --steps=0. With --timeout=0 that leaves only time and memory as failure modes. The cost is that results no longer reproduce deterministically.

None of this proves completion "in every case". The evidence is observed, not proved, and per-check difficulty does grow with context, so some admitted program could still need more than any fixed budget. Treating that as a resource failure is a policy statement. The compiler can make it true only by removing the fixed knobs; no measurement can guarantee it.

items.current_bound: 100,000 normalized steps per prover per VC (z3 rlimit 80,450,000; alt-ergo --steps-bound 100000; cvc5 --rlimit)

premises: Proof completion (gnatwhy3 plus cvc5/z3/alt-ergo) is a trusted external tool premise. Everything here is observation on one host (Linux x86_64, 22 CPUs, 31 GB, no swap) under concurrent load from the T2 (Lean, up to 15 GB) and T3 (flow-mode gnatprove, up to 3.8 GB) tracks. Timings are contaminated and are not benchmarks.

Programs larger than 4096 bytes are not admitted (silver check rejects them: 'source is outside the Silver catalogue'). They were built only from blocks that are admitted on their own, every block wrapped and checked (200 of 200 Accepted). The F3 block is validated by the accepted 1 KB, 2 KB and 4 KB F3 programs. The 4 KB-or-smaller composites f1-1024/2048/4096, f2-1024/2048/4096 and f3-1024/2048/4096 were accepted in full. The scaling results therefore represent the admitted fragment without the 4096-byte and 63-operator limits; they are not results about currently admitted programs.

The three families do not cover every admitted shape: no argument-input shell, no dynamic-length String guards, no maximal 64-leaf expressions at scale. Per-check difficulty for other shapes may grow differently.

The earlier 4 KB measurements I reused (static800, dynamic769, dense-distributed63, program-40oTy6) were made with -j0 and, for larger-expressions, the vendor gnatprove through dev.py rather than the Image adapter. Their report statistics (per-check steps and time) are comparable; their wall times are not directly comparable to mine.
Reading the alt-ergo/CVC5 'High failure' results as memory-limit kills is plausible but not verified (sampled RSS 0.905 GiB against a 1000 MB limit).

recommendations: Replace '--memlimit=1000' in src/silver.adb:121 with an explicit host-derived value, such as MemTotal in MB set at bootstrap in Silver_Build. Do not use --memlimit=0: at --level=2 it silently becomes 1000 MB. This removes a fixed prover cap that is already making alt-ergo fail at 32 KB.

Make the step budget non-binding: either '--steps=0' (confirmed unlimited) or a two-stage run that retries with --steps=0 only when the first run leaves checks unproved. Keep '--timeout=0'. Document that proof can then end only through time or memory exhaustion, and that results may differ by host.

Keep wording like language.md:499-500 ('sufficient host resources ... operational premises'). Add the measured scaling: roughly quadratic time, and quadratic gnatwhy3 memory for dense straight-line code. Add host guidance: a 31 GB host handles dense code up to roughly 8 KB, about 9 GB per dense 4 KB measured. Mixed or looping code reaches 32 KB in about 5 GB.

Note that -j has almost no effect on the dominant cost, because one gnatwhy3 process per subprogram does nearly all the work. To grow the envelope, consider later having the emitter cut the VC context (Assert_And_Cut, or splitting Main into local subprograms). That is a design change with its own proof obligations, not a limit.

Optionally widen Silver_Image_Model.Original_Node_Id (src/silver_image_model.ads:5) to the 63-bit Byte_Count range, so the adapter has no fixed parse cap that could in principle be reached before resource exhaustion.

The production compile's report reader has to handle main.spark sizes that grow linearly at about 1.4-2.2 KB per check: 1.43 MB at 4 KB dense and 1.01 MB at 16 KB F2. Coordinate with the report-capacity track: a fixed 16 MiB buffer would become the next fixed cap at larger sizes.

track: T5 — Oracle, assurance and validation consequences of a resource-exhaustion failure model
summary:
I found no Oracle sentence that requires a size cap. oracle.md:19 only requires that any limit which exists be explicit and have a documented purpose. oracle.md:10 keeps rejection limited to explicit, decidable rules. oracle.md:11 and :25 let "sufficient host resources" stand as a documented assumption about trusted tools and the OS.

So the owner's model can be adopted without an Oracle amendment, provided three things hold:
(a) Resource failure is never reported as rejection (status 2) or as success (status 0).
(b) Every solver limit that Silver itself configures stops being binding. Today the 100,000-step and 1,000 MiB per-prover caps are Silver policy, so reaching them counts as a proof failure. Under oracle.md:14 that is an implementation defect, not an environmental outcome.
(c) Real hard limits in the pinned tools stay as explicit language rules, following the B1 precedent.

Source review and T3's gcc probes found three hard limits in GNAT 16.1. All are out of reach today only because of the 4096-byte source cap:
- A line may be at most 32,765 columns after tab expansion (tab stops every 8).
- An identifier longer than 4096 characters crashes GNAT ("Name buffer overflow", then a GNAT bug box).
- An exponent of 800,000 or more is a hard error ("exponent too large").

GNAT's fixed internal ID ranges (names, strings, nodes, source positions) also mean one source-size bound derived from the tool is needed. That bound replaces 4096; it is not an arbitrary knob.

The Lean ToolContract already states the weak premise. Current.lean:221 reads `boundedProofCompletes : ∀ checks, BoundedFragment checks → ∃ steps, tools.prove checks steps`, with no numeric bound. The numbers appear only in prose: assurance.md:590-592, trusted-boundary.md:43 and :901-907, and language.md:757-760.

What changes for real:
- **The premise gets stronger.** Under the 4096 cap the set of admitted programs, and so of proof goals, is finite. Without the cap, the completion premise covers infinitely many goals of unbounded size. It then rests on the solvers behaving as decision procedures for the generated fragment.
- **Size-specific Lean proofs must become symbolic.** `uniformRangeObligations` is proved with `decide +kernel` at 4096, and `guaranteedIntegerLast` is 32767.
- **The compiler must size its storage from the input.** Today a fixed buffer overflow is reported as "Rejected" (status 2).

Recommended design:
- **Escalating proof limits.** Geometric step and memory tiers, ending in a non-binding tier. A ladder is needed rather than one unlimited run because GNATprove tries its provers in turn, so one unlimited prover can starve the others. The ladder stops early only when every prover gives a definite non-resource answer. That outcome is prover incompleteness and remains a defect.
- **A new exit status 4 for resource exhaustion**, separate from 2 (rejected) and 3 (defect).
- **Validation by universal Lean proofs plus tool-limit boundary tests and scaling runs at several sizes**, instead of 4096 boundary tests.

Order: finish the B1/M1 repair (#77-#84; integrated checkpoint still pending) first, then the escalation and diagnostics work, explicit tool-derived rules, compiler internals that scale with input, Lean parameterisation, removal of the language caps, and finally the String value/argument domain. Lifting that domain to Integer'Last changes observable behaviour (4097-byte arguments are now rejected at runtime with status 1 and would become valid input). Oracle line 18 permits this as an explicit pre-1.0 change.
